NUEVA YORK — Los Yankees se han pasado casi todo septiembre organizando a los lanzadores para la fase de octubre.
Gerrit Cole está en la lista para ser el lanzador titular en la Serie de Comodín. Cam Schlittler se ha ganado un sitio en esa misma conversación.
Max Fried vuelve a la rotación, mientras que Carlos Rodón y Will Warren están en la lista para lanzar como relevos una vez que empiece la postemporada. Estas decisiones han dejado poco margen para que algún aspirante de última hora se cuele de nuevo en el grupo de titulares.
Eso limitó las opciones de Clarke Schmidt incluso antes de que volviera a incorporarse a la plantilla. Su regreso tras una segunda operación de Tommy John nunca se planteó con el objetivo de volver a alcanzar el volumen de trabajo de un lanzador titular en las dos últimas semanas.
Los Yankees lo incorporaron al plantilla el 16 de septiembre para aportar duración, lanzamientos certeros y una variedad de lanzamientos propios de un abridor desde el bullpen. No había jugado en las Grandes Ligas desde el 3 de julio de 2025, y solo había lanzado siete entradas en las ligas menores durante su rehabilitación.
Schmidt volvió esa noche en Minnesota y consiguió dos outs, permitiendo dos sencillos de rebote y ponchando a dos. Fue su primera aparición en las Grandes Ligas en 14 meses y medio. Y lo más importante para los Yankees es que supuso el inicio de una prueba para un papel que requiere una rutina diferente.
En lugar de un día fijo de salida y una larga preparación previa al partido, Schmidt ahora tiene que entrar en calor rápidamente, salir al campo en medio de la acción o en una entrada limpia, y recuperarse siguiendo el horario de un relevista.
La situación de la plantilla ya no dejaba margen para que volviera a la rotación. Según las previsiones actuales de la MLB para la postemporada de los Yankees, Cole, Schlittler y Fried figuran como titulares, mientras que Schmidt, Rodon y Warren están entre las opciones de relevo.
Aaron Boone ha confirmado que Cole será el lanzador titular en una posible serie de comodín. Warren tiene prevista una última salida como titular en la temporada regular antes de pasar al bullpen. La posibilidad de que Schmidt volviera a ser titular se había convertido en algo más teórico que práctico para este octubre.
Un problema en el bíceps interrumpe la única prueba que le quedaba a Schmidt
Esa diferencia se hizo aún más evidente el domingo en Arizona. Clarke Schmidt estaba calentando para lo que habría sido su segunda salida desde la operación cuando notó un calambre en el bíceps derecho durante la derrota de los Yankees por 8-4 ante los Diamondbacks en el Chase Field. Dejó de lanzar y no llegó a salir al campo.
Los Yankees dijeron que las pruebas de fuerza no indicaban ningún problema en el hombro ni en el codo. Se espera que Schmidt vea a un médico del equipo en Nueva York, sin que, por el momento, se hayan previsto más pruebas.
Schmidt explicó por qué se negó a seguir adelante a pesar de esa sensación tan pronto después de la operación. Respondía a la pregunta de si ese episodio sugería un contratiempo estructural.
«No es nada estructural, fue más bien por precaución», dijo Schmidt. «Obviamente, dadas las circunstancias, al estar recuperándome de una operación, no quiero forzar nada. Todas las pruebas salieron bien, ni el hombro ni el codo presentan problemas. Era más bien una sensación parecida a un calambre. No he tenido ningún problema al atrapar la pelota hoy por la mañana y en los últimos días me he sentido muy fuerte. Así que fue algo muy, muy leve, solo por precaución».
Boone dijo que Schmidt no pudo terminar su calentamiento a pesar de haber superado las pruebas iniciales.
«Espero que no sea nada grave, pero sí lo suficiente como para que no entre en el partido», dijo Boone. «Ya veremos qué pasa».
En su lugar, Tim Hill lanzó la sexta entrada. Los Yankees habían conseguido una ventaja de 4-1 gracias a los jonrones de Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. y Spencer Jones en la tercera entrada, antes de que Arizona anotara cinco carreras en la quinta, coronadas por el grand slam de Nolan Arenado ante Brent Headrick. Justin Martínez se llevó la victoria, Headrick la derrota y no se acreditó ningún salvamento.
Un historial de 67 partidos como titular se enfrenta a un futuro repleto de jugadores en los Yankees
Schmidt ya ha demostrado que puede ser titular en las Grandes Ligas. Según los registros de la MLB, 67 de sus 97 partidos como profesional han sido como titular. Tiene una efectividad de 3,82 en 393 1/3 entradas y registró una efectividad de 3,32 en 14 partidos como titular en 2025, antes de que un problema en el codo le obligara a dar por terminada la temporada.
La pregunta es si los Yankees todavía tienen un hueco real en la rotación de titulares para él. Según los registros públicos de contratos, Cole y Rodon tienen contrato hasta 2028 y Fried hasta 2032. Schlittler se ha consolidado como lanzador titular de primera línea, mientras que Warren sigue bajo el control del club. Schmidt podrá acogerse al arbitraje en 2027 y podrá convertirse en agente libre tras esa temporada.
Las reacciones en Internet pasaron rápidamente del domingo al invierno. Los aficionados se preguntaban por la resistencia de Schmidt, cómo encajaría junto a Luis Gil y si los Yankees podrán contar con él para lanzar entradas decisivas en octubre.
Ningún responsable de los Yankees ha dicho que Schmidt no vuelva a ser titular en Nueva York. Pero la profundidad de la rotación, su plazo de recuperación y los planes de los Yankees para la postemporada lo han dejado relegado a un segundo plano, con tantas opciones de titulares que ya no puede seguir siendo tu opción predeterminada.
Los Yankees necesitan que Schmidt demuestre que la transición al bullpen funciona
Por eso es tan importante lo del bíceps, aunque las noticias médicas sigan siendo positivas. Schmidt no está intentando llegar a los 90 lanzamientos. Lo que quiere es demostrar que puede calentar rápido, salir al campo cuando lo necesiten y recuperarse para otra salida.
La transición ya ha dado lugar a dos momentos incómodos. Schmidt calentó el sábado por la noche, pero Boone se decantó por Michael Fulmer en la novena entrada de un partido empatado. Fulmer encajó el jonrón de dos carreras de Pavin Smith que decidió el partido. El domingo, Schmidt estuvo a punto de salir al campo, pero unos calambres se lo impidieron.
Los Yankees tienen un balance de 89-66, a seis partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando quedan siete partidos por disputar, según la clasificación de la MLB. Ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y ocupan el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana. Su última semana empieza el martes en el Yankee Stadium contra los Rays.
Si Schmidt pasa la prueba, esos partidos supondrán un reto más sencillo. Su objetivo inmediato ya no es volver a ganarse un puesto en la rotación. Se trata de demostrar a los Yankees que pueden confiar en él en el bullpen cuando empiece octubre.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- It has felt inevitable that the American League East race would be decided this week in the Bronx.
The Rays have led the Majors’ most competitive division for most of the season, and they haven’t ceded the top spot in the standings since reclaiming first place on June 27.
But the Yankees have always been there -- threatening and falling back, perhaps -- but never trailing by enough to diminish the potential importance of this week.
Well, here it is.
The Yankees will host the Rays in a four-game series at Yankee Stadium, beginning with a separate-admission doubleheader on Tuesday. Thanks to the Rays’ terrific homestand and the Yankees’ series loss in Phoenix, the question now is how much longer this race will remain alive.
The Rays arrived in New York holding a six-game lead in the division race with only seven games remaining. One victory by Tampa Bay will eliminate the Yankees from the AL East race and lock them into an AL Wild Card spot. So for the Yankees to have any chance, they must pull off a four-game, three-day sweep.
The stakes? As Gerrit Cole once said, “They’re high.” Let’s dive in.
What’s at stake?
Rays: Winning just one game will guarantee the Rays’ first AL East championship since 2021, giving them a bye through the Wild Card Series and home field advantage in both the AL Division Series and -- if they advance -- the AL Championship Series. They also need just one win to clinch the season series against the Yankees.
Yankees: Manager Aaron Boone acknowledges that it would be a “tall order” to keep the Rays from spraying bubbly in the Bronx, but that’s exactly what they intend to do. They entered the season looking to change the narrative after coming up short in their pursuit of the Blue Jays last year. They’re instead on the verge of settling for another consolation prize and needing to fight through a best-of-three.
How are the starting rotations lined up?
Rays: They will send their two best starters to the mound for Tuesday’s doubleheader. First comes veteran right-hander Nick Martinez, their clubhouse leader and most dependable source of innings. Tampa Bay has a 22-7 record behind Martinez this season. Then comes Drew Rasmussen, one of the AL’s top starters. The Rays haven’t lost one of Rasmussen’s starts since July 9, going a perfect 11-0 in his outings since then. Martinez will be pitching with an extra day of rest, while Rasmussen will be working on four days’ rest for only the seventh time this season. Left-hander Ian Seymour and right-hander Freddy Peralta would be in line to start Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
Yankees: Carlos Rodón and Max Fried will start the doubleheader, in that order. Both have dealt with injuries this season but are rounding into form at the right time. In three September starts, Rodón is 2-0 with a 2.08 ERA, putting a bout with left elbow inflammation into his rear-view mirror. After twice landing on the injured list with a bone bruise in his pitching elbow, Fried is 1-0 with a 1.69 ERA in three September starts. Cole and AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler follow in the third and fourth games of the series, respectively.
What has been going well for each team lately?
Rays: Um, everything? The Rays just went 8-1 during their final regular-season homestand, and they’ve won four straight series against the Braves, Astros, A’s and Red Sox. Since getting swept in a four-game series at Fenway Park coming out of the All-Star break, they’ve put together a 39-18 record -- the best in baseball since July 20. Their starting pitching has been particularly strong, with a 2.81 ERA this month that ranks second to only the Yankees. They have found different ways to score runs, as usual, including early rallies like Sunday and a pair of walk-off homers from AL MVP candidate Junior Caminero.
Yankees: These Yanks suddenly find themselves leaning on the strength of their pitching, believing the offense will eventually deliver. Ben Rice cracked his team-leading 39th home run, fulfilling a prediction Boone made in Spring Training. Rice said Boone was teasing him, coming up “one or two” short of his preferred total, so look for Rice to swing for his 40th this week. Austin Wells has hit three homers in his last six games, while Heliot Ramos has homered in his last two games. He could be an important piece if the Yankees are going to make October noise.
What are some areas of concern that could be an issue this week or in the postseason?
Rays: Plenty of Rays have picked up the slack, but leadoff man Yandy Díaz has had a tough month, with a .229/.286/.357 slash line in September. He sets the tone for their lineup, so it’s obviously important for him to be in top form come October. And this is really nitpicking, considering he’s 3-0 with a save and a 1.42 ERA this month, but MLB saves leader Bryan Baker has more walks (four) than strikeouts (two) in seven September appearances. He’ll need to be lights-out in the postseason, too.
Yankees: Other than Aaron Judge’s right calf strain, which the Yankees are treating like a top-secret matter of national importance, there are concerns bubbling about the state of the bullpen. Brent Headrick’s velocity has dipped and he may be showing fatigue after a Major League-leading 79 appearances. Tim Hill hasn’t been the automatic ground-ball machine of years past. Michael Fulmer gave up a game-winning homer in Arizona. But there’s no bigger issue than proving they can win without Judge, the engine around which their offense is built. They are 48-41 without him, compared to 41-25 with him.

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees fans are frustrated. It's been 17 long years since they've enjoyed a parade down the Canyon of Heroes following a World Series victory. The man primarily responsible for that frustration is general manager Brian Cashman.
If you ask veteran MLB insider Ken Rosenthal, though, Cashman is doing a bang-up job. Rosenthal gushed about Cashman during a recent appearance on Foul Territory.
"It's time, it's past time, to understand what [Brian] Cashman has accomplished," Rosenthal said. "And all of those years finishing above .500, since 1998, yes, they have had financial advantages, too. So have a lot of other teams. No other team has had a winning record every year.
"Now I know, certain fans, certain Yankees fans, will say, 'No World Series title since 2009.' Yes, that is true. It's undeniable, and some of the teams have not been constructed as well as they could've been. I would expect Cashman would say that as well. However, they are always in the mix."
He went on to acknowledge what the standard is in New York - World Series or bust - and he detailed that through line from George Steinbrenner to Derek Jeter to Aaron Judge. But ultimately, his point was that the playoffs are random and that Cashman shouldn't be held accountable for not winning a ring since 2009. Regular season greatness, in Rosenthal's opinion, is a better measuring stick of a GM's abilities.
Sounds ridiculous, right? Even if we grant him that the World Series is tough to win, and it is, that's the point! We're still looking at a clear decline. Think back to the dynasty that began in 1996. The Yankees won four World Series, yes, but they had also lost two others (2001, 2003), meaning that during an eight-year stretch they made it to the final showdown six times. Now consider that since 2009 they only have one World Series appearance to their credit: the 2024 defeat at the hands of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
It's hard not to see a distinct break. Remember, too, that Cashman ascended to the role of general manager on February 3, 1998. He's not fully responsible for those championship clubs, as they had been molded and shaped by Gene Michael and Bob Watson before him.
Also remember that during the 2008-2009 offseason, Cashman's seat was scorching hot, and he was basically mandated by George to go on the huge spending spree that netted New York CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira, and A.J. Burnett. If his hand hadn't been forced, we likely wouldn't have seen those splashes, and we don't have the ring to show for it.
An honest assessment of Brian Cashman's Yankees tenure pegs him as a middle-of-the-pack general manager
Going back to Rosenthal for a second, he's also been on an apology tour for Cincinnati Reds president of baseball operations, Nick Krall. Krall runs a small-market team, but he enjoys having an MVP-caliber player in Elly De La Cruz, a young ace in Chase Burns, and the likely NL Rookie of the Year in Sal Stewart on pre-arb contracts. That trio makes up just under $2.5 million of Cincinnati's $133 million payroll. He could've set the remaining $130 million on fire and gotten better results.
I bring this up as a reminder that insiders like Rosenthal's sole job is to get inside information and break stories. They get that by cultivating relationships, so when you hear them give an edgy or unconventional opinion, it's because they don't want to hurt a source's feelings.
This isn't to say that Cashman is a bad GM. He's made his share of great moves. He's made blockbuster trades like acquiring Alex Rodriguez, Giancarlo Stanton, and Juan Soto. He's found diamonds in the rough like Brent Headrick (and several others).
But the issue with Cashman is that he doesn't learn from his past mistakes. After failing to acquire prime Johan Santana to protect Phil Hughes, Joba Chamberlain, and Ian Kennedy, he let Ivan Nova, Eduardo Nunez, and Adam Warren stand in the way of trading for Cliff Lee a few years later. Then he compounded the mistake when he failed to sign Lee the following offseason.
In recent years, he's failed to capitalize on Aaron Judge being the literal reincarnation of Babe Ruth by shying away from emptying out the farm to acquire difference makers who would have changed the Yankees' calculus.
It's impossible to look at his missteps and not see titles left on the table. It's criminal that he's enjoyed the best hitter this generation has produced, yet since 2017 has just one World Series appearance to show for it.
Go back to the 1998 team. That should have been his lesson. That club laid waste to the American League, winning 114 games. Entering October, a World Series berth felt inevitable. Going into the World Series against the San Diego Padres, the only question was whether the Yankees would hoist the Commissioner's Trophy after four games or five.
Since those glory days, winning the division is no longer a guarantee. Making the playoffs has sometimes felt like it's on shaky ground. The standard has been lowered, but by the organization, not the fans.

item.content:encoded:
Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality.
“Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East.
Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium this week, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday.
Aaron Boone acknowledged that his team will probably have to sweep the Rays just for a crack at the division crown, as FanGraphs gave the Yankees a measly 2.7% chance of winning the AL East before Sunday’s game.
“There’s still a chance,” Cam Schlittler said, “but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
While the Yankees still technically have a shot to defy the odds, the far likelier scenario is that their postseason begins on Sept. 29 at home against Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
With that in mind, let’s try to predict what the club’s roster could look like for that series.
Hitters (15): Ben Rice, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, Ryan McMahon, George Lombard Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., José Caballero, Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez, Anthony Volpe, Amed Rosario
With the Yankees providing minimal info on Aaron Judge’s calf strain, it can’t be assumed he’ll be available.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return from a sprained thumb as soon as Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trent Grisham is still in play as a playoff option as he recovers from a hamstring strain, but Boone said that activating him before the end of the regular season is “complicated,” partly due to roster logistics.
With Max Schuemann presumably the corresponding move for Chisholm, the Yankees would have to option someone else if they activated Grisham before the playoffs. That someone wouldn’t be able to be recalled for 10 days barring a new injury; it seems like Jasson Domínguez is being protected from that window in case he’s needed for the Wild Card roster.
Grisham has been doing baseball activities and is “pretty deep into his running progression,” Boone said. If he is on the Wild Card roster, the Yankees will have an interesting decision to make between him and Spencer Jones in center field.
Third base could also be a conundrum, as Ryan McMahon and José Caballero don’t offer much offensively, and Amed Rosario is a poor defender. He’s only on the roster as an option against lefties, even though he hasn’t been great against them.
Another idea would be to use Volpe, who has been playing second, at third against lefties since he played a few games there in the minors this season. However, he doesn’t have a strong arm, and he hasn’t been working at third base since being recalled. Volpe said that the Yankees have not talked to him about manning the hot corner before the regular season ends.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we’ll figure out as the week unfolds how I want to play it.”
Volpe can also play second over Chisholm against lefties.
Pitchers (11): Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Clarke Schmidt, John Schreiber, Tim Hill, Ryan Weathers
As things stand, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler are scheduled to pitch against the Rays, in that order. That would give Cole, who has struggled to get swing-and-miss, an extra day of rest if he were to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young frontrunner, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1.
Because the Wild Card round is a best-of-three series, Rodón isn’t needed, especially with Will Warren expected to work out of the bullpen and able to provide length.
Warren, slated to make one more start this season after struggling on Sunday, is one of a few converted starters who could impact the Bombers’ bullpen this postseason. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are the others. Schmidt, being cautious in his return from Tommy John surgery, couldn’t come into Sunday’s game due to some bicep cramping, while Weathers isn’t expected to return from a flexor strain before the regular season ends.
Still, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled out the idea of Weathers’ first game back coming in the playoffs.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”
As for the relievers that the Yankees have leaned on all season, David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick headline the group. All have been used heavily, especially Headrick.
The lefty allowed a grand slam to Nolan Arenado and saw his fastball velocity down an average of 1.3 mph during his major league-leading 79th appearance on Sunday, but he insisted that he feels fine physically. Boone also downplayed concerns over Headrick’s ongoing velocity fluctuations, though he did say that he hopes to get him and other relievers “in a good spot” with some rest ahead of the playoffs.
That said, the Yankees still haven’t been eliminated from the AL East race. They’ll keep trying to take the division from the Rays until they are.
“We’re going to show up Tuesday,” Boone said, “and try and kick their butt.”

PHOENIX — Los Yankees se fueron del Chase Field con el tipo de derrota que cambia el panorama de la última semana.
El domingo, Nueva York tuvo a Corbin Burnes contra las cuerdas, remontó un déficit inicial y se puso con una ventaja de 4-1 gracias a tres jonrones en la tercera entrada. Heliot Ramos empató el partido con un jonrón solitario. George Lombard Jr. sumó un jonrón de dos carreras, y Spencer Jones conectó otro justo después de él. Burnes se fue del partido tras 2 2/3 entradas.
La ventaja inicial no duró mucho. Will Warren llenó las bases con un out en la quinta entrada, y el bullpen de los Yankees no pudo evitar que Arizona le diera la vuelta al partido. Brent Headrick ponchó a Geraldo Perdomo y luego concedió una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll con las bases llenas. Nolan Arenado siguió con un grand slam ante una bola rápida de cuatro costuras a 94,2 mph, dando la vuelta a un marcador de 4-2 y poniendo a los Diamondbacks por delante 6-4. Arizona sumó dos carreras más en la séptima y ganó 8-4.
Los Yankees perdieron dos de tres partidos en Arizona y ahora tienen un balance de 89-66. Tampa Bay mejoró su balance a 95-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a seis partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando quedan siete partidos por disputar. Los Rays llegan al Yankee Stadium para una serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes con una doble jornada dividida. Una sola victoria de Tampa Bay en la serie dejaría a los Yankees fuera de la lucha por el título de la división.
Ese contexto hizo que las declaraciones del entrenador tras el partido tuvieran más peso que un simple intento de pasar página. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el club tiene que encontrar el equilibrio entre una lucha por el título de división que se va desvaneciendo y proteger a un cuerpo de lanzadores muy castigado, además de preparar una plantilla plagada de lesiones para octubre.
La afirmación de Boone choca con la clasificación
A Aaron Boone le preguntaron cómo se enfrentarían los Yankees a Tampa Bay y si el hecho de que la lucha por el título de división se esté desvaneciendo podría cambiar su forma de gestionar los minutos de juego. Su respuesta incluyó una amplia defensa de cómo ha respondido su equipo durante una temporada llena de lesiones y una importante racha negativa este verano.
«Y hemos estado a la altura en casi todas las ocasiones», dijo Boone.
Esa es la parte que llama la atención del mensaje de Boone. Aaron Judge estuvo más de tres meses de baja por una lesión en las costillas, volvió el 8 de septiembre y luego volvió a entrar en la lista de lesionados por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. Además, Nueva York sufrió una racha de siete derrotas seguidas durante un tramo de 4 victorias y 14 derrotas, antes de recuperarse y asegurarse una plaza en la postemporada.
El final del partido en Arizona fue el contrapunto. Los Yankees llegaron a la quinta entrada con una ventaja de tres carreras y la terminaron perdiendo por dos. No anotaron nada después de la tercera y encadenaron dos derrotas seguidas tras ganar el primer partido del viernes por 9-2.
Las cifras cuentan dos historias diferentes sobre los Yankees
La clasificación de la MLB a fecha de 21 de septiembre muestra por qué Boone puede hablar de una temporada sólida, mientras que la tabla de la División Este de la Liga Americana presenta un panorama más sombrío.
Los Yankees han marcado 137 carreras más que sus rivales, frente a la diferencia de +83 de Tampa Bay. Según las previsiones de la MLB, Nueva York debería tener un balance de 92-63, tres victorias más que su balance real. Sin embargo, los Rays llevan una ventaja de seis partidos.
Nueva York tiene un balance de 33-32 contra equipos con un porcentaje de victorias igual o superior al 50 %. Tampa Bay tiene un balance de 37-25 en esos partidos. La capacidad de los Yankees para anotar y evitar carreras sugiere que son un equipo más fuerte de lo que indica su segunda posición en la clasificación, pero los Rays han sabido convertir los partidos difíciles en victorias con mayor consistencia.
Ese contraste es lo que le da tensión a la afirmación de Boone. Los Yankees se han recuperado de rachas perjudiciales, pero no con la frecuencia suficiente como para controlar la división de cara a la última semana.
Boone lanza un mensaje contundente a los Rays
Boone también dejó claro que no ve el martes como una puesta a punto inmediata de cara a la postemporada. Dijo que las decisiones sobre el descanso pueden dejarse para más adelante, una vez que los Yankees se enfrenten por primera vez al equipo al que llevan meses persiguiendo.
«Pero lo primero es lo primero: el martes vamos a salir al campo e intentar darles una buena paliza. Así de sencillo. Y lo mantendremos así de sencillo», dijo Boone.
A Tampa Bay le falta una victoria contra los Yankees para asegurarse el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Nueva York tiene que ganar los cuatro partidos para mantener vivas sus opciones de cara al último fin de semana.
Eso hace que Boone tenga que gestionar dos frentes a la vez. A los Yankees aún les queda una posibilidad matemática de ganar la división, pero la plantilla para la postemporada, la carga de trabajo del bullpen y los jugadores lesionados se están convirtiendo en las preocupaciones más prácticas de octubre. Nueva York también empieza la semana ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
La carga de trabajo de Headrick añade urgencia a la decisión de Boone
La 79.ª salida de Headrick el domingo fue la segunda más alta de las Grandes Ligas. La velocidad media de su bola rápida fue inferior a la de esta temporada, aunque él lo achacó a la ejecución más que al cansancio.
Los Yankees han confiado en Headrick durante toda la temporada. El domingo quedó claro lo rápido que esa fortaleza puede convertirse en un motivo de preocupación en octubre. Se encontró con las bases llenas, estuvo a un out de salir del apuro, pero luego concedió la base por bolas y encajó el golpe decisivo de Arenado.
Boone dijo tras la derrota que el descanso podría formar parte del plan una vez que se decida el campeón de la división. Eso podría pasar ya el martes.
Hasta entonces, su postura pública está clara. Los Yankees no van a ceder la serie ante Tampa Bay, ni siquiera después de que el colapso de Arizona haya dejado la clasificación prácticamente decidida. La gran afirmación de Boone es ahora lo que los Yankees deben demostrar en el campo: tras decir que han sabido hacer frente a la adversidad en casi todas las ocasiones, su próxima prueba llega con los Rays en posición de celebrar la victoria en el Yankee Stadium.

The New York Yankees led 4-1 after three innings on Sunday in Arizona. Three home runs off Corbin Burnes had knocked the Diamondbacks starter out of the game and given the lineup exactly the kind of start it needed.
None of it held. A five-run fifth inning turned a comfortable lead into a deficit, and the Yankees fell 8-4 at Chase Field to drop two of three in the series. New York is 89-66 and now sits six games behind the Rays in the American League East with seven to play.
After the game, manager Aaron Boone met with the media and offered an honest assessment of how it all fell apart.
Boone on Warren’s Start
Will Warren carried a 4-1 lead into the fifth inning before things unraveled. Warren allowed three consecutive baserunners in the fifth, loading the bases with one out, and Boone pulled him for Brent Headrick.
Boone’s evaluation was measured. He saw a pitcher whose stuff was there but whose command slipped at the wrong time.
“Early on he was in the strike zone really well and getting a lot of first pitch strikes ahead,” Boone said. “His stuff was again good. I feel like it’s been in a good place for the last three or four weeks now, but just started falling behind a little bit there in the latter part of the game.”
Warren had retired hitters efficiently through four innings, but back-to-back frames in which he fell behind multiple hitters proved costly. The stuff did not abandon him. The execution did.
The Offense Went Quiet
The Yankees scored all four of their runs in the third inning. Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. all connected off Burnes to build what felt like a comfortable lead.
After that, nothing. The Diamondbacks’ bullpen shut the door, and the lineup could not find a way to respond after the fifth-inning collapse.
“They’ve got a good relief corps. Obviously a lot of big arms,” Boone said. “I thought we had some decent at-bats along the way, but just obviously weren’t able to build on the lead or crawl our way back in.”
A Late Concern Emerges for the Yankees
Boone also provided an update on Clarke Schmidt at the end of his postgame session.
“He felt some cramping in his bicep when he was warming up, so obviously he didn’t want to take any chances there,” Boone said. “He checked out pretty well afterwards and all the strength tests. And so I’m hoping it’s not a big deal. But enough to have him not go into the game.”
Final Word for the Yankees
The Yankees blew a three-run lead and dropped a series they needed. The division is slipping away. The bullpen showed cracks on a day where the workload caught up with one of its most reliable arms.
Boone was honest about all of it. Warren’s stuff was good but the execution faltered. The offense disappeared after the third inning.
The Rays come to the Bronx on Tuesday for a doubleheader. The margin for error is gone.

PHOENIX — Una sola entrada convirtió una serie fuera de casa que los Yankees parecían dispuestos a salvar en una derrota que les acompañó hasta su regreso al Bronx.
El domingo, en el Chase Field, Nueva York llegaba a la parte baja de la quinta con una ventaja de tres carreras. Para cuando terminó la entrada, Nolan Arenado ya había dado la vuelta a las bases, Arizona había anotado cinco veces y los Yankees se habían quedado atrás para siempre, acabando por perder 8-4 ante los Diamondbacks.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 89-66 y a seis partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays, cuando solo quedan siete partidos por jugar. Además, esto puso fin a una gira por Arizona con un balance de 1-2, después de que Nueva York empezara la serie con una victoria por 9-2 y luego perdiera dos veces en partidos que se decidieron en los últimos compases.
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y siguen ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana. Pero la última semana tiene ahora un carácter de urgencia diferente. Tampa Bay puede hacerse con el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana con una sola victoria en la serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes en el Yankee Stadium.
El domingo también se prolongó el drástico cambio de rumbo tras el partido inaugural del viernes. El sábado terminó con un jonrón decisivo de Pavin Smith contra Michael Fulmer. El último partido trajo consigo otro fallo del bullpen, pero el mismo perjuicio en la clasificación.
Una entrada de cuatro carreras debería haber cambiado el rumbo de la tarde
Arizona se adelantó en el marcador gracias a un sencillo impulsador de Geraldo Perdomo en la primera entrada. A partir de ahí, Will Warren se asentó en el montículo, impidiendo que los Diamondbacks ampliaran su ventaja hasta la cuarta entrada y dando tiempo a la alineación para atacar a Corbin Burnes.
Ese ataque llegó de repente en la tercera entrada.
Heliot Ramos empató el partido con su decimotercer jonrón. George Lombard Jr. le siguió más adelante en la entrada con un jonrón de dos carreras, el quinto de la temporada.
El batazo de Lombard recorrió, según las estimaciones de Statcast, 424 pies, el jonrón más largo de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas.
Spencer Jones conectó un jonrón justo después, su undécimo. A continuación, lanzó una bola que se calculó que recorrió 448 pies. Los dos jonrones de los novatos sumaron un total de 872 pies.
Los Yankees habían pasado de ir perdiendo 1-0 a ponerse 4-1 por delante y habían obligado a Burnes a abandonar el partido tras solo 2 2/3 entradas. Parecía el tipo de remontada de los jóvenes que podría sacar adelante a una alineación en la que faltaban los titulares lesionados.
En cambio, esas cuatro carreras fueron toda la producción ofensiva de los Yankees.
Diecinueve outs demuestran lo mucho que ha dado un giro el partido
Cinco relevos de los Diamondbacks sumaron entre todos 6 1/3 entradas sin encajar carreras tras la salida de Burnes. Los Yankees solo consiguieron tres hits contra ese grupo y no anotaron en las últimas 19 eliminaciones.
Justin Martínez lanzó una quinta entrada sin permitir carreras y se llevó la victoria, mejorando su balance a 3-0. Brent Headrick cargó con la derrota, quedando con un balance de 7-4. No se concedió ningún salvamento.
Los Yankees terminaron el día con 216 jonrones, liderando la Liga Americana, pero su poderío no pudo compensar el colapso que vino después.
Warren y Headrick pierden el quinto
Warren llegó a la quinta entrada defendiendo la ventaja de 4-1. Lars Nootbaar conectó un doble, Ketel Marte un sencillo y Gabriel Moreno recibió una base por bolas, llenando las bases con un out. Aaron Boone recurrió a Brent Headrick, uno de los lanzadores del bullpen más utilizados por los Yankees.
Headrick ponchó a Perdomo y luego concedió una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll con las bases llenas, dejando el marcador en 4-2. Arenado mandó una bola rápida justo fuera por la línea del jardín izquierdo antes de conectar con fuerza el siguiente lanzamiento para un grand slam, dando a Arizona una ventaja de 6-4.
Headrick disputaba su 79.ª salida, la segunda cifra más alta de las Grandes Ligas, y, según se informó, la velocidad media de su bola rápida estaba aproximadamente 1,3 mph por debajo de su media de la temporada.
Headrick dijo que el problema era la precisión, no el cansancio.
«Me sentí bien, pero me faltó precisión y me quedé atrás respecto a los bateadores», dijo Headrick.
Warren se fue del partido con cuatro carreras encajadas, seis hits y tres bases por bolas en 4 1/3 entradas. Boone ha dicho que Warren hará una salida más como titular en la temporada regular contra Baltimore antes de pasar al bullpen en octubre.
Warren apoyó al relevo que se hizo cargo de la situación complicada que él había dejado.
«Nos ha dado un montón de problemas todo el año», dijo Warren. «Es un rollo, pero está claro que contamos con él, y nos ha ido muy bien con él todo el año, y va a seguir haciéndolo bien».
Arizona sigue sumando mientras el bullpen de los Yankees flaquea
Perdomo impulsó una carrera con un triple ante John Schreiber en la séptima entrada, y Carroll le siguió con un sencillo impulsor que dejó el marcador final en 8-4. Arizona terminó con siete carreras sin respuesta y se aseguró su 47.ª victoria tras remontada, la mejor marca de la MLB.
Los Yankees también se quedaron sin poder ver a Clarke Schmidt en el bullpen, como tenían previsto. El lanzador diestro tuvo que dejar de calentar por unos calambres cerca del brazo que se le había operado. Las primeras pruebas de fuerza fueron alentadoras, y se esperaba que Schmidt fuera examinado una vez que el equipo volviera a Nueva York.
Por qué esta podría ser la derrota más cara de los Yankees en 2026
Tras dos derrotas seguidas en Arizona, los Yankees vuelven al Yankee Stadium con Tampa Bay en condiciones de zanjar la lucha por el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana en el campo de Nueva York.
El daño va más allá de haber desperdiciado una ventaja. El Tampa Bay llega ahora al Bronx y solo necesita una victoria en la doble jornada del martes para asegurarse el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana, ya que esa victoria también le garantizaría el desempate en la serie de la temporada.
Eso da lugar a la consecuencia más incómoda del colapso de Arizona: los Yankees podrían verse obligados a ver cómo los Rays celebran el título de división en el Yankee Stadium, en el mismo campo donde Nueva York esperaba mantener viva la lucha hasta la última semana.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

(Photo credit: Arianna Grainey)
Nolan Arenado hit his third grand slam of the season to cap a five-run fifth and the Arizona Diamondbacks kept their slim National League wild card chances alive with an 8-4 victory over the New York Yankees on Sunday in Phoenix.
Geraldo Perdomo had two hits and two RBIs and five Arizona relievers limited the Yankees to three hits in 6 1-3 scoreless innings as the D-backs scored the final seven runs for their major league-leading 47th comeback win.
Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones homered for the Yankees, who fell six games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East. The Yankees lead the American League with 216 homers. Lombard had two hits.
Lars Nootbaar and Gabriel Moreno had two hits and scored twice and Ketel Marte had two hits for the Diamondbacks, who have won two straight games.
The D-backs (82-74) remained five games behind NL wild-card leaders Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres (both 87-69) and four behind the Philadelphia Phillies (86-70) with six to play.
The D-backs would lose a tiebreaker to the Cubs, and tiebreakers against the Padres and Phillies have yet to be determined. The D-backs end the season with three games at Colorado and the final three at San Diego.
Justin Martinez (3-0), the second Arizona reliever to follow Corbin Burnes, struck out two in the fifth for the victory.
The Yankees lost their second straight after winning four of five.
Nootbaar started the D-backs' five-run fifth with a one-out double off Yankees starter Will Warren. Marte singled and Moreno walked to load the bases. Brent Headrick (7-4) entered and struck out Perdomo before walking Corbin Carroll to force in a run.
Arenado followed with his 381-foot homer into the Arizona bullpen for a 6-4 edge. He has five homers in his last 10 games and is tied with Houston's Yordan Alvarez for the major league lead in grand slams.
Perdomo tripled in a run and scored on Carroll's single in a two-run seventh.
The D-backs took a 1-0 lead in the first on singles by Nootbaar, Marte and Perdomo. Warren gave up six hits and four runs in 4 1/3 innings, with three walks and four strikeouts.
Ramos, Lombard and Jones homered four batters apart in a four-run third off Burnes for a 4-1 lead. Ramos homered with two outs before Luis Garcia Jr. singled and Lombard and Jones hit back-to-back shots. Lombard's went an estimated 424 feet. Jones' went 448.Burnes gave up four runs and five hits, with two walks and two strikeouts in 2 2/3 innings. He has given up nine runs and five homers in 10 1-3 innings of three starts since returning after a 15-month absence after Tommy John surgery.

It's no secret that Yankees left-handed relief pitcher Brent Headrick has been one of, if not their most dominant relief pitcher this season in 2026. However, concerns are growing about Brent Headrick as we approach the final week of the regular season before the postseason.
Yankees beat writer Brendan Kuty of The Athletic posted earlier this evening in a tweet that "Headrick's average fastball velocity tonight in Arizona against the Diamondbacks was 92.9 mph, which Kuty cites as 1.3 mph slower than his 'season average of 94.2 mph."
Headrick Gave Up Grand Slam In 8-4 Loss In Arizona
Headrick came into this game with the bases loaded and two outs; he proceeded to walk in a run facing right fielder Corbin Caroll, and then gave up a grand slam to D-Backs third baseman Nolan Arenado to go from a 4-1 Yankees lead to then a 6-4 D-Backs lead, a game in which they would go on to win 8-4. Oddly enough, the pitch before Arenado just pulled foul down the left field line, only to hit a grand slam that stayed fair on the very next pitch to left field.
Headrick has been phenomenal this year with a 7-4 record and a 2.10 ERA in 79 appearances. His ERA has been under 2 for much of the season, but in his last seven games, he's struggled with a 4.76 ERA in 5.2 innings of work. However, for much of the 2026 season, Headrick's ERA has been under two. The concerning part is that Headrick looks worn out. Pitching in so many crucial games this year, when the Yankees were tied or in a close game, has forced the organization to rely on Headrick a lot.
It makes sense why Headrick's velocity, therefore, would be down a bit, per Kuty's tweet. If the Yankees want to win a World Series, they will need not only significant contributions from key players in the lineup, but also from the bullpen, on which they've relied heavily: the trio of closer David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, and Brent Headrick.
Headrick's breakout 2026 campaign with the Yankees and his story are a rather interesting one. The Yankees claimed Brent Headrick off waivers in February 2025 from the Minnesota Twins. Before joining the Yankees, Headrick pitched to a 5.97 ERA with the Twins in 15 games spanning 2023-24.
Yankees Likely To Rest Headrick Before Playoffs
Headrick's usage for the rest of the regular season and then the postseason, likely a Wild Card matchup between the Yankees and Red Sox, will be something to monitor moving forward. If the Yankees want to win a World Series this year, they will have to rely heavily on Brent Headrick, as they have throughout the 2026 season, to get an opportunity in the postseason.
The challenge will also be longer, since the Yankees will likely have to come out of the Wild Card. The Yankees now have their final two regular-season matchups: four games against the Tampa Bay Rays, then three against the Baltimore Orioles. The Wild Card series begins on Tuesday, September 29th, as the Yankees will look for more of the Brent Headrick they've seen for much of the 2026 season and not the version they saw of him today.

In the final game and rubber match of their three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks (82-74), the Yankees (89-66) coughed up an early lead to lose 8-4.
Here are the takeaways...
-- Will Warren got the nod to start the game, and delivered a solid outing... until the fifth inning. Up to that point, Warren had allowed one earned run - an RBI single in the first inning by Diamondbacks shortstop Geraldo Perdomo - and struck out four batters through four full innings. The Yankees entered the fifth inning leading 4-1 (thanks to home runs from Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr., and Spencer Jones), but after Warren surrendered two hits and a walk to load the bases with just one man out, he was pulled in favor of left-handed reliever Brent Headrick.
-- Headrick struck out Perdomo to record the second out, but he couldn't close the door on the frame, issuing a free pass to Corbin Carroll to bring in one run before surrendering a grand slam to Nolan Arenado which gave Arizona a 6-4 lead.
-- Of those five earned runs surrendered in the fifth, three were attributed to Warren, and two to Headrick.
-- New York's right-handed reliever John Schreiber allowed two more runs in the seventh inning, surrendering a triple to Perdomo and a single to Carroll which brought the shortstop home. For Arizona, former Yankee Jonathan Loáisiga recorded the final six outs, facing the minimum six batters without allowing a run to wrap up the 8-4 loss.
Game MVP: Nolan Arenado
Arenado's grand slam flipped the game on its head, and the massive momentum-shifting blast gave the Snakes a lead they wouldn't relinquish.

What's next
The Yankees travel back home on Monday and will kick off a pivotal three game series against the AL East divisional leading Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday at 1:05 p.m.
Of course, now 6.0 games back of Tampa Bay for first place in the AL East with just seven regular season games remaining, the Yankees need a miracle to win the division.
Carlos Rodón (2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP in 76.1 IP) is set to take the mound for the Yankees.

It’s Sunday once more, and you know what that means — it’s time for our weekly social media roundup! This weekend has been yet another veritable whirlwind in the Bronx, as the team celebrated a postseason appearance, bid farewell to a fan favorite, closed an era of minor league baseball, and watched as their Captain hit the shelf once more. With so much in store, let’s get started!
Another Celebration in Minnesota
It was deja vu all over again! For what feels like the fifty millionth time, the Yankees celebrated in Minnesota, as they clinched a postseason berth earlier this week with a victory over their favorite AL Central punching bag.
The Roberto Clemente Award
This week, the New York Yankees named Carlos Rodón their nominee for the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award. The team honored the Rodón Foundation, which sets out to help families suffering with fertility issues.
In Service
Yankees reliever Brent Headrick welcomed Henry Ledlowe from his hometown in Illinois to the Bronx, courtesy of the National Down Syndrome Society. Unfortunately, the Instagram post cannot be embedded, but can be found here.
The Jazz Chisholm Jr. Foundation, meanwhile, marked the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
Where’s Oswaldo? Unfortunately, Cincy.
This week, the Yankees designated fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment in order to make room on the 40-man roster for Clarke Schmidt. Unfortunately, he was claimed off waivers by the Cincinnati Reds, and while we’re all excited to see him (hopefully) get some regular playing time — as he was very much blocked in the Bronx — it will be sad to see the human golden retriever, well-loved by the fans and players alike, in a different uniform.
A testament to his popularity is the fact that the Yankees, RailRiders, Patriots, and YES Network all posted farewells to him on their social media accounts. David Cone also came back to Twitter briefly in order to wish him well.
Farewell to the RailRiders
Starting next year, the Yankees’ Triple-A affiliate will undergo its second rebrand since joining the Yankees family, abandoning the RailRider moniker in exchange for a new nickname which has yet to be revealed. PHOENIX — Both the Yankees and Rays saw their respective games end in walk-off fashion on Saturday, but only one of the division rivals emerged victorious.
It wasn’t the Yanks, who suffered a 5-3 loss to the Diamondbacks when Michael Fulmer surrendered a game-ending, two-run home to Pavin Smith with one out in the ninth inning. Aaron Boone said that he considered using Clarke Schmidt, one game back from Tommy John surgery, instead, but he went with the journeyman Fulmer because he’s had more experience in those situations.
“I just felt like Fulmer’s been in these spots and throwing the ball really well for us, and Smith got him there,” Boone said of the reliever, who has a 3.09 ERA this season.
Meanwhile, at Tropicana Field, the Rays pulled off a 2-1 win over the Red Sox thanks to a bloop single from Richie Palacios in the ninth. Tampa now has a five-game lead over the Yankees with just eight games left in the regular season.
The American League East foes will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium from Sept. 22-24, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday. Boone acknowledged that his club will probably have to sweep the Rays for a crack at a division title.
“We sweep, then it gets interesting,” the manager said with the Yankees’ postseason ticket already punched.
But the odds are already stacked against the Yankees with the team finishing its series in Arizona on Sunday. They entered Saturday with a just a 2.8% chance of winning the division, according to FanGraphs.
Making matters tougher is that the Rays, owners of the AL’s best record, currently lead the season series between the two teams, 6-3. There’s also the fact that the Yankees will be without Aaron Judge, who returned to the injured list with calf strain on Saturday.
“They’re playing tremendous baseball, so it’s tough to climb up in the standings when they keep winning,” Cody Bellinger said after going 0-for-4 on Saturday. “So mathematically, it’s pretty tough, but gotta keep on rolling.”
“We gotta go on a good run. It’s gonna be tough,” added Cam Schlittler, who allowed one earned run over six innings but committed a costly error on Saturday. “I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job with it. So there’s still a chance, but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
The good news for the Yankees is that their best starters are lined up to face the Rays. While they haven’t officially announced their probables for the series, it looks like Max Fried and Carlos Rodón will pitch the doubleheader before Gerrit Cole and Schlittler, the Cy Young frontrunner, close out the four-game set.
The Rays, however, are set to throw a few of their best with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez, Ian Seymour and Freddy Peralta slotted for the highly-anticipated matchup.
While they’re not officially out of the division race yet, the likeliest scenario is that the Yankees end up hosting Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year. It is not where the team wants to end up after finishing 2025 with the same record as the Blue Jays but losing the season series tiebreaker, but Bellinger remained confident that the Yankees can still win their first title since 2009.
“Obviously, the goal is to win the division, rest your guys, get those extra off days,” he said. “That’s always goal No. 1. Ultimately, World Series champions have come out of the Wild Card.”

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se pasaron casi toda la noche del sábado lidiando con dos realidades en el Chase Field. Cam Schlittler volvió a ofrecerles una gran salida, pero cada entrada cobró más importancia después de que Tampa Bay ya se hubiera llevado la victoria con un tanto decisivo en la última entrada.
Nueva York tuvo la oportunidad de evitar que sus cada vez más remotas opciones en la División Este de la Liga Americana se le escaparan aún más. En cambio, los Yankees se fueron con una derrota por 5-3 ante los Diamondbacks de Arizona, lo que amplió su desventaja en la división a cinco partidos cuando solo quedan ocho por disputar.
Los Yankees hicieron lo suficiente para que el partido se pudiera ganar. Ben Rice conectó un fly de sacrificio en la quinta entrada. Heliot Ramos y Austin Wells conectaron jonrones en la sexta. Schlittler superó su primer bajón serio en el control en semanas y terminó seis entradas concediendo solo una carrera limpia.
Arizona siguió respondiendo. Jordan Lawlar neutralizó la primera ventaja de Nueva York con un triple de dos carreras en la quinta entrada, después de que Schlittler fallara al intentar atrapar un toque. Corbin Carroll empató el partido con un fly de sacrificio en la sexta entrada, tras dos bases por bolas y un sencillo de toque que llenaron las bases.
Lo que estaba en juego ya estaba claro antes del primer lanzamiento. Varios jugadores de los Yankees vieron desde el vestuario de visitantes cómo Tampa Bay vencía a Boston por 2-1, un resultado que situaba a los Rays cinco partidos por delante. Nueva York había ganado ocho de sus últimos diez partidos, pero la racha de Tampa Bay casi no dejaba margen para perder otra oportunidad.
A continuación, los Yankees contaron con dos entradas sin puntos de su bullpen. Brent Headrick consiguió dos outs en la séptima antes de que Paul Blackburn terminara esa entrada y se encargara de la octava. El marcador se mantuvo en 3-3, lo que dejaba a Nueva York a una entrada limpia de tener otra oportunidad al bate.
Schlittler había hecho lo suficiente para mantener a los Yankees en el partido. Cedió tres hits y tres carreras, solo una limpia, y se anotó seis strikeouts en 98 lanzamientos. Su promedio de carreras limpias bajó a 1,94. Para entonces, el margen de error era ya casi nulo.
Fue entonces cuando el partido dio un giro con la decisión más decisiva de Aaron Boone de toda la noche respecto al bullpen.
Boone recurre a Fulmer con el partido en juego
Boone le pasó la parte baja de la novena a Michael Fulmer en lugar de al cerrador David Bednar. Fulmer había lanzado dos tercios de una entrada sin encajar carreras en la victoria del viernes por 9-2, mientras que Bednar no había lanzado desde que hizo dos entradas el miércoles en Minnesota.
Fulmer parecía haber eliminado a Ildemaro Vargas con un strikeout en un lanzamiento con cuenta completa, pero Vargas impugnó la decisión a través del sistema automático de bolas y strikes de la MLB. El lanzamiento se consideró bola, lo que le dio a Arizona una base por bolas para abrir el turno.
Fulmer ponchó a Lawlar. A continuación, Pavin Smith entró como bateador suplente y mandó el segundo lanzamiento de Fulmer, un «cutter», 391 pies al campo derecho para un jonrón de dos carreras que dio la victoria.
Juan Morillo se llevó la victoria para Arizona, mejorando su balance a 5-4. Fulmer sufrió su primera derrota y vio cómo su promedio de carreras limpias subía de 1,59 a 3,09. No hubo salvamento.
La decisión llamó la atención porque Bednar llegaba a la noche con 34 salvamentos y una efectividad de 2,58. Fulmer, fichado por los Yankees a finales de agosto, solo había lanzado 11 1/3 entradas en las Grandes Ligas esta temporada antes del sábado y sigue formando parte de un bullpen muy concurrido de la postemporada.
Schlittler asume la culpa tras una racha irregular
Un error de Schlittler en la quinta entrada ayudó a Arizona a anotar dos veces, y ocho lanzamientos seguidos fuera de la zona al inicio de la sexta propiciaron la remontada que empató el partido. Se recuperó ponchando a Nolan Arenado y a Tim Tawa con dos corredores en posición de anotar.
El lanzador diestro se centró en su propio error tras el partido.
«Asumo toda la culpa por eso», dijo Schlittler. «Cometí un error ahí y dejé que nos marcaran dos carreras. Así es el béisbol, pero esa la tengo yo».
Schlittler ha cedido una carrera limpia o menos en 24 salidas como titular, lo que le convierte, junto a Sandy Koufax y Bob Gibson, en uno de los únicos lanzadores de la Era de la Bola Viva con al menos 24 salidas de este tipo en una temporada, sin contar los «openers».
El descanso de Bednar acentúa el contraste en el bullpen
La secuencia de relevos de los Yankees ofreció un anticipo de la postemporada. Headrick y Blackburn sumaron entre ambos dos entradas sin encajar carreras antes de la novena. Bednar no llegó a salir, mientras que Fulmer lanzó dos días seguidos.
Fulmer llegaba al sábado con una ERA de 1,59 y había limitado a sus rivales a un promedio de bateo de 0,171 en sus apariciones con los Yankees. La diferencia en la carga de trabajo era aún más marcada: Fulmer había lanzado el viernes, mientras que Bednar había tenido dos días completos de descanso tras su salida de dos entradas del miércoles.
Esto es importante ahora que los Yankees están reorganizando una plantilla de lanzadores que se reducirá de cara a octubre. Bednar es una opción consolidada para las últimas entradas. Fulmer ha lanzado lo suficientemente bien como para seguir en la pugna por un puesto en la plantilla, pero su puesto está menos asegurado, ya que varios relevistas compiten por las limitadas plazas de la postemporada.
El sábado supuso otro momento de evaluación, y esta vez se dio en un momento de máxima presión.
Los Yankees pierden más terreno antes del enfrentamiento con los Rays
Con esta derrota, los Yankees se quedan con un balance de 89-65. Tampa Bay sube a 94-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a cinco partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees siguen teniendo una ventaja de 5 partidos y medio sobre Boston en la lucha por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
Boone reconoció lo estrecho que se ha vuelto el camino con cuatro partidos contra Tampa Bay a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium.
«Si les barreríamos, entonces la cosa se pondría interesante», dijo Boone. «Pero no puedes barrerlos antes del partido [del domingo]».
Los Yankees cierran la serie contra Arizona el domingo, con Will Warren como lanzador previsto para enfrentarse a Corbin Burnes. Tras el partido del sábado, Nueva York debe mantener viva la lucha por el título de división y, al mismo tiempo, decidir en qué relevos confía Boone cuando llegue la próxima novena entrada empatada.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.content:encoded:
The St. Louis Cardinals missed the playoffs this season and will need to head back to the drawing board to build a team that can qualify for the postseason next year.
Moreover, the question is what moves they should make to improve the team to challenge the Chicago Cubs and Milwaukee Brewers in the NL Central.
It’s been a wild 2026 MLB season for Anthony Volpe, who was optioned to Triple-A in August and then recalled in September. Still, it might be in the 25-year-old’s best interest to get a fresh start elsewhere.
Since reaching the majors in 2023, Volpe has been hitting .225 with 432 hits, 54 homers, 218 RBIs, and 241 runs scored in 537 games for the New York Yankees in his career, per StatMuse.
Despite this production during his four seasons in Pinstripes, FanSided’s Robert Murray believes that the Cardinals could be the change of scenery that Volpe needs after a rollercoaster career with the Yankees.
“Anthony Volpe would be a really good, buy-low option for the Cardinals,” Murray wrote in a Sept. 19 article. “Volpe was supposed to be the Yankees’ long-term answer at shortstop. Instead, he struggled mightily and fluctuated between the majors and minors.
“The Yankees still believe in Volpe and want to hold him, so a trade might be considered unlikely. But this is something that other teams will sniff around this offseason, I believe, and Bloom – who has previously worked with the Red Sox and Rays – should have plenty of familiarity in dealing with the Yankees.”
Anthony Volpe Could Boost Trade Value In the Coming Weeks
Since being recalled on Sept. 9, Volpe has performed well. Entering Sept. 20, Volpe has been batting .290 with nine hits, a home run, seven RBIs, and four runs scored in seven games, per StatMuse.
Moreover, if Volpe can end the season on a high note and have a productive postseason, his trade value might increase, and a team like the Cardinals could feel they can tap into his potential.
Volpe will have an opportunity to step up like every Yankee in that lineup, given that Aaron Judge is back on the injured list. New York can’t replace Judge with one batter, but they can do so with everyone chipping in.
Cardinals, Yankees Get Compelling Trade Idea
Recently, Christopher Kline of FanSided floated a trade idea that would send Volpe along with LHP Brent Headrick and LHP Kyle Carr to the Cardinals for 24-year-old shortstop Masyn Winn.
“The Yankees’ lack of fundamental soundness on the defensive end has bitten them in the you-know-what all season, just like it did last year,” Kline wrote in a Sept. 16 article. “The hope was that top prospect George Lombard Jr. could steady the ship at shortstop, but he has stacked up errors left and right.
“It’s too early to write off the 21-year-old long term, but he could serve more comfortably at third or second — which is notable, since Jazz Chisholm Jr. is about to [be a free agent]. Winn immediately alleviates a ton of defensive issues for the Yankees, while his weaker bat would be well-protected in the American League’s most potent lineup.”

item.content:encoded:
Friday was a bad day for the New York Yankees even though they opened their final road series of the regular season with a blowout win (NYY 9, ARI 2). Captain Aaron Judge is less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him more than three months. Judge's status for the rest of the season is up in the air.
"I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires," manager Aaron Boone said (via MLB.com). "... The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
The Yankees are always cagey about Judge's injuries. They declined to reveal the severity of the calf strain or give a timetable for his return. Generally speaking, Grade 1 calf strains (the least severe) require 2-3 weeks on the injured list, though calves are very tricky and easy to reinjury. They must be allowed to heal fully, otherwise you risk a more severe injury.
For all intents and purposes, the Yankees are locked into the top wild-card spot. They're six games up in the loss column on the Boston Red Sox, who currently sit in the second wild card spot, plus the Yankees won the season series and have the tiebreaker, so it's really a seven-game lead. New York can clinch the top wild-card spot as soon as Sunday.
The AL East title remains mathematically possible, but it is a long shot. The Yankees are four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the loss column with four head-to-head games remaining next week in the Bronx. The Rays only need to win one of those four games to clinch the season series and secure the tiebreaker, upping the difficulty for New York.
Just to lay it all out, here's what needs to happen for the Yankees to win the AL East, assuming they sweep those four games against the Rays and clinch the tiebreaker for themselves, which is a pretty big assumption:
- Rays go 6-3 or better: Rays win AL East
- Rays go 5-4: Yankees must go 9-0
- Rays go 4-5: Yankees must go 8-1
- Rays go 3-6: Yankees must go 7-2
- Rays go 2-7: Yankees must go 6-3
- Rays go 1-8: Yankees must go 5-4
- Rays go 0-9: Yankees must go 4-5
The Yankees have already clinched a postseason spot and winning the AL East was a long shot even with Judge. These last nine regular-season games are almost meaningless. If the AL East race gets interesting in a few days, the Yankees can shift gears, but the big picture takes priority this next week. Resting key relievers, lining up the rotation for the Wild Card Series, etc.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game," Cody Bellinger said (via MLB.com). "For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I'm fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win, and beat anybody."
With the postseason less than two weeks away, Judge's calf injury creates a lot of questions for both him and the Yankees overall. Here are three questions for the man himself, and his team.
Three questions for Judge
1. Will he return for the postseason? This is really the only question, right? The Yankees are built around Judge being the best hitter in the world, and when he's not, the walls begin to cave in. New York had one of the lowest-scoring offenses in baseball when Judge was out with his rib injury. To paraphrase another New York baseball legend, Judge is the straw that stirs the drink.
Judge is eligible to come off the injured list next Sunday, the final day of the regular season. Roster-wise, he can return in time for the postseason. Health-wise, we have no idea. Calf strains are rarely 10-day absences, but that's what the Yankees have to hope is the case here. There's a very real chance the Yankees are without Judge for at least the Wild Card Series, and maybe longer.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason,” Aaron Judge said. “That’s definitely the plan.”
Said the calf strain involves the soleus muscle — which he said is more crucial to running and hitting — making it more difficult to play through.
2. Will he be himself at the plate? Judge did not go on a minor-league rehab assignment before returning from the rib injury and it showed. He went 4 for 23 (.174) with one walk and 13 strikeouts in his seven games back before the calf injury. His timing was not there at all. Judge's one homer came on a hanging breaking ball. Otherwise, pitchers threw fastballs by him consistently.
To put a number on it, Judge missed with 41% of his swings against fastballs in his seven games back, more than double the 19% league average. This is what it looks like when you miss with more than two out of every five swings against heaters:
It is not exactly a surprise a hitter who did not go on a rehab assignment after spending more than three months on the shelf looked out of sorts at the plate. Judge and the Yankees knew it would take him some time to get back up to speed at the plate, and they were willing to live with it. The goal was always to be ready for the postseason, not so much the regular season.
These last nine games aren't particularly important for the Yankees in the standings, but they were incredibly important to Judge. He needed at-bats to rediscover his timing at the plate, and get back to being the dominant hitter he's been throughout his career. The calf strain puts that on pause. Judge now has even fewer at-bats available to get back to being himself.
3. Will he be able to play the field? There is a scenario in which Judge plays through the calf strain as a full-time DH who doesn't run at 100% (or close to it). How the Yankees would align their defense in that scenario, I have no idea. Ben Rice is a full-time DH these days and also New York's best non-Judge hitter. Platoon-mates Luis Gárcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt are first basemen.
Unless the Yankees do something unexpected, like put Gárcia back at second base (where he was terrible defensively) or Rice back behind the plate (where he was also terrible defensively), slotting Judge in at DH means one of the team's most productive hitters will have to sit. This is something the Yankees will worry about when the time comes, and not a second sooner.
Three questions for the Yankees
1. Where will the righty pop come from? The Yankees have a very lefty-heavy lineup and Judge's righty heft provides important balance. Only the Cleveland Guardians have gotten fewer plate appearances from righties this season. Friday's lineup against Arizona Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodriguez could be what the Yankees run out there against lefties in October:
- 1B Paul Goldschmidt, RHB
- LF Cody Bellinger, LHB
- RF Heliot Ramos, RHB
- DH Ben Rice, LHB
- 3B Amed Rosario, RHB
- CF Spencer Jones, LHB
- SS George Lombard Jr., RHB
- C Austin Wells, LHB
- 2B Anthony Volpe, RHB
Goldschmidt and Ramos are lefty mashers. Bellinger and Rice are very productive left-on-left hitters. Jones has performed well against lefties as a big leaguer, though his minor-league track record against southpaws isn't great. Rosario is having his worst season against lefties. The 7-8-9 spots are unlikely to make an impact offensively, regardless of the pitcher's handedness.
That lineup would look much more imposing with Judge in the No. 3 spot. Perhaps this is not such a big concern though? Since trade deadline day, the Yankees have the highest batting average (.289) and on-base percentage (.362) against lefties, and the third-highest slugging percentage (.456) despite Judge not playing much, and not being much of a factor when he did play.
In all likelihood the Yankees will host the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, and Boston has three quality lefty starters (Jake Bennett, Ranger Suárez, Payton Tolle) and a shutdown lefty relief tandem (Aroldis Chapman, Erik Miller). To beat the Red Sox, the Yankees will need their righty hitters to produce, and now the status of their best right-handed hitter is in question.
2. Will the pitching hold up? Despite not having Judge for more than three months, the Yankees have the American League's best run differential (+143) and second-best record (89-64). They can thank their pitching staff. New York has allowed only 3.68 runs per game this year, the fewest in baseball. Since trade deadline day, it's an incredible 3.37 runs allowed per game.
There are some cracks beginning to form, however. Gerrit Cole has surrendered eight home runs in his last three starts, including five on a four-seam fastball that is no longer the dominant pitch it was at his peak. Max Fried's velocity has been down a tick since returning from a bone bruise in his elbow late last month. That injury has sent him to the injured list twice this year.
Cam Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, has thrown a career-high 184 ⅔ innings with two regular-season starts remaining, plus the postseason. Key late-inning relievers Paul Blackburn, David Bednar, and Brent Headrick have worked a lot -- A LOT -- this season and have all shown a slight dip in velocity in recent weeks, which perhaps is a sign the workload is catching up to them.
Without Judge (and sometimes even with him), the Yankees are a run prevention team. Their superpower is a suffocating pitching staff that is among the best in baseball at limiting hard contact, particularly in the air. With Judge absent, the pitching staff and the ability to prevent runs in general will be of paramount importance. No Judge reduces the margin of error considerably.
3. What about their other injured players? Judge is not the only injured Yankee. Center field Trent Grisham has not played since Sept. 4 due to a Grade 2 hamstring strain. On Friday, Boone said Grisham is pretty far into his running program, and he could make it back before the end of the regular season. That would give the outfield a lift should Judge miss extended time.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. has not played since jamming his thumb sliding into second base on Sept. 8. Boone said Chisholm will come off the injured list when the Yankees return home next week. He's had a down year overall, but Chisholm was playing his best baseball of the season right before the injury. He's an important presence given his speed and defense in particular.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers is working his way back from a flexor strain. He last pitched Aug. 22. Weathers is throwing bullpen sessions, though Boone confirmed he won't return during the regular season. If/when Weathers does return, it will be as a reliever. He has bullpen experience and the Yankees could use middle relief help, but Weathers has to make it back first.
At minimum, Chisholm and Grisham would give the Yankees more options for their Judge-less lineup, even if they only platoon. It wouldn't be hard to find a role for Weathers, who had allowed no more than one run in six of his last seven starts before the injury. Bottom line though, the Yankees need Judge. Everything else is secondary to his return and effectiveness.

Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster.
After New York clinched a playoff spot, Yankees analysts Bryan Hoch and Patrick Donnelly of MLB.com revealed the likely playoff roster, and they didn't have Volpe on it.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Aaron Judge, Heliot Ramos
DH: Ben Rice
SP: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole
RP: David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Tim Hill, Ryan Yarbrough, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, Ryan Weathers, Will Warren
The Yankees leaving Volpe off the playoff roster would be a disappointing outcome for the shortstop. It also could signal the end of his tenure in New York as Lombard is the shortstop of the future.
Volpe is hitting .253 with 2 home runs and 26 RBIs this season with the Yankees.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot as New York will be hosting a Wild Card series again.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
However, despite clinching a playoff spot, the Yankees made it clear the job isn't finished. New York likely won't win the AL East again, which is frustrating, but the Yankees have confidence they can go on a deep playoff run.
The Yankees are 88-64 and 5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the AL East.
